about: The day's turn as a wait comes to it (Wait until first light, Wait until dark): told by where the company waits (out under the sky, indoors, under the ground) and, out of doors, by the sky (fair, grey, rain, fog, wind, cold, hot, ash; cold in winter and in frost country). One sentence or two, and never the same morning twice running while there is another (the boredom census, BO-08: 'The sky greys, then lightens. It is morning.' 23 times in eight walks). And the night sky watched for its own sake (kind sky: Lie back and watch the sky, Fun Friday 20 November): told by the weather (sky), the sign riding this month (riding: yes, with {sign} and {signline}, only where the company reads the stars) and whether one of the company was born under it (own: yes, with {who}; mine, one who came alone), the moon by its phase ({moon}), all read from the sky instrument (Instruments.night); nothing gained but the half hour.

lines.text: The sky greys, then lightens. It is morning.
The stars go out one by one, and the east turns pale. It is morning.
A bird starts up, then another. The light comes grey, then gold, and it is morning.
The sun comes up red over the edge of the land. It is morning, and the dew is down.
Morning comes clear and still. Your shadow is long on the ground before the sun is a hand high.
The dark thins to a grey morning. There is no sunrise to speak of.
Morning comes under low cloud, the same grey from edge to edge.
Morning comes slowly behind the rain.
It is morning, and still raining. Everything you own is damp.
It grows light, but the fog does not lift. Morning is a whiteness ten paces off.
The fog turns from black to grey to white. Above it, it is morning.
The wind keeps on through the last of the night, and the morning comes up hard and bright.
Morning comes with the wind still blowing, and the clouds going fast overhead.
Morning comes with frost white on everything, and your breath smoking in the first light.
It is a cold dawn. The ground is hard, and your hands are slow to wake.
The sun is up early, and already warm on your face. It is morning.
Morning comes brown and dim through the falling ash.
Grey light shows at the cracks of the shutters. It is morning.
Outside, a cock crows, and the light comes in grey under the door.
The room comes out of the dark a thing at a time. It is morning.
There is no dawn down here. By the count of the hours, it is morning above.
Nothing changes in the dark under the ground, but the night is over, up above.
The hours of the night go by. By your own reckoning it is morning.
The light goes. It is dark.
The light goes yellow, then grey, and then it is dark.
The sun goes down, and the dark comes up out of the ground to meet the sky.
The first star comes out, then all of them. It is night.
The grey day goes to a grey dusk, and then to dark.
The rain goes on into the dark, and you can hear it but not see it.
The fog darkens around you until there is nothing to see at all. It is night.
The wind gets up as the light goes. It is dark.
The cold sharpens as the light goes. It is dark, and freezing.
The heat goes out of the day at last. It is dark.
The brown light goes, and the ash goes on falling in the dark.
The light at the window goes, and the room is dark.
The cracks of the shutters go from gold to grey to nothing. It is dark.
Down here nothing changes, but by the count of the hours it is night above.
The hours go by. By your own reckoning it is night.
The stars come out thick. The longer you look, the more there are. High in the south, {sign} is riding. {Signline}
You find {sign} at last, low over the roofs. Once you have seen its shape you cannot unsee it. A star falls, and only you see it.
{Moon} hangs over the roofs, and the sky turns slow as a mill-wheel. {Sign} climbs out of the east and stays.
Overhead, {sign} is riding: the stars {who} was born under. {Signline}
There is {sign}, plain as a lantern. Old wives say a sign shines brightest over those born under it. Tonight it is easy to believe, for {who}.
Overhead, {sign} is riding: the stars you were born under. {Signline} It seems a fair thing to have said of you.
There is {sign}, plain as a lantern, your own sign. Old wives say it shines brightest over those born under it. Tonight it is easy to believe.
The stars come out one at a time, then all at once. There are shapes in them that someone who knew the stars could name. You lie and look anyway.
{Moon} rides over the roofs. A bat crosses it, then another. The half hour goes by like a held breath.
The sky is enormous and very quiet. A dog barks across the river, and stops. You do not think of anything at all for a while.
Cloud lies over everything. Once it thins, and for a breath you see a few stars where {sign} should be. Then it closes again.
Cloud lies low, lit faintly by {moon} behind it. There is nothing to see. It is restful all the same, the dark and the ground at your back.
The fog takes the roofs, then the trees, then the ground a yard away. You lie in a small grey room of your own. It is very quiet.
The clouds move fast and low. A gap opens, and for a moment there is one bright star in it. Then it is gone, like a word half heard.
Rain finds your face before you find a single star. You lie there a while anyway. Then you sit up, dripping, and oddly pleased.
The rain is soft and steady. You pull your hood over your face and listen to it on the cloth. It is the best roof there is, for a while.
No stars tonight, only rain on the leaves and the gutters running. Down the street a door bangs, and a woman laughs. You stay until you are soaked.
There are no stars, only a dull red smear where the ash hangs. A flake drifts down and settles on your eyelid like warm snow.
